title: Question 14735
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Source row: BARMATRIX Q#14735 is a Criminal Law / Other Crimes item. The original row reports 81% correct, choice A as both the official key and 81% selection, with B/C/D selected at 8%/7%/4%. It tests accomplice liability for theft where the passenger saw the theft only as it happened and lacked intent to promote it.  The requested reasoning posture was also reviewed; it emphasizes preserving the ambitious goal while keeping candor about what is proved versus inferred.

Final variation:

After a church-league softball game, Peter drove Timothy home. They stopped at an all-night convenience store for gas. Timothy offered to pay for the gas. While Timothy pumped gas, he was surprised to see Peter enter the store, take cash from an unattended drawer, and return to the car. Timothy paid Lydia, the attendant, for the gas, and Peter drove away. Peter offered to reimburse Timothy for the gas, but Timothy declined. After Lydia discovered the missing cash, she called the police, and the car was later stopped. Peter escaped with the stolen cash and was never prosecuted.

If Timothy is prosecuted for theft as an accomplice, should he be convicted?

---
call: If Timothy is prosecuted for theft as an accomplice, should he be convicted?

choices.A: No, because Timothy had no intent to promote the commission of the offense.
choices.B: No, because Peter, the principal, was never prosecuted.
choices.C: Yes, because Timothy facilitated commission of the offense by failing to make any effort to stop it.
choices.D: Yes, because Timothy paid Lydia for the gas while he knew Peter was holding the stolen cash.

rightExplanation:
A is correct. Timothy is not guilty as an accomplice because the call asks whether he is liable for theft as an accomplice, and the stem gives no purposeful participation in Peter’s theft. He was surprised by the theft. He paid only for the gas. He declined reimbursement. Nothing in the stem shows that Timothy intended to promote or facilitate Peter’s theft.

Gold Key: Accomplice liability requires intent or purpose to promote or facilitate the crime. Mere presence, silence, failure to stop the principal, or after-the-fact knowledge is not enough.

Silver Key: In accomplice-liability answer arrays, separate mental-state answers from conduct-only answers. The conduct-only answers are tempting, but the call is asking whether this person joined the crime.

---

wrongExplanations.B: It uses a principal-status trap. Whether Peter was prosecuted is not the deciding question. Gold Key: The principal’s non-prosecution does not itself block accomplice liability. The real missing piece is Timothy’s intent to promote or facilitate the theft.
wrongExplanations.C: It uses moral-common-sense bait. Timothy’s failure to stop Peter does not supply the mental state required for accomplice liability. Gold Key: Accomplice liability needs intent to promote or facilitate, not merely a failure to intervene. Silver Key: This is a conduct-only answer. It talks about what Timothy did not do, but the call turns on whether Timothy joined the crime.
wrongExplanations.D:
It proves only after-the-fact knowledge plus an innocent payment for gas. That does not show that Timothy intended to help Peter commit the theft. Gold Key: Knowing about the theft after it has begun, without purposeful aid to the crime charged, does not make Timothy an accomplice to the theft.

---.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: — principal-status bait. The answer tries to make Peter’s prosecution status dispositive. That is a fabricated requirement, but the student needs the Gold Key to cut it safely.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: — wrong element. It proves failure to intervene, not intent to promote the theft.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: — wrong element / wrong timing. It proves payment for gas while aware of the cash, not purposeful assistance in the theft.

c3.label: Residual A
c3.text:
— the only answer that names the missing element: Timothy had no intent to promote the offense.

---

studentScript: Accomplice call. I need intent to promote. Timothy was surprised and only paid for gas. B is principal-status bait. C and D are conduct-only traps. A.

A.signal: Only answer that names the missing mental-state gate: intent to promote.
A.lawyer: Accomplice liability requires participation plus intent/purpose to facilitate the offense; the stem negates prior knowledge and purposeful assistance.

B.signal: The answer makes Peter's non-prosecution dispositive, but the call is Timothy's accomplice liability.
B.lawyer: Modern accomplice liability does not require prosecution or conviction of the principal; Standefer confirms an aider-and-abettor may be convicted despite the principal's acquittal.

C.signal: It talks about failure to stop Peter, not Timothy's intent to promote the theft.
C.lawyer: Mere presence, silence, or failure to stop a crime is not enough for accomplice liability without the required intent.

D.signal: It proves knowledge while paying for gas, not intent to help commit the theft.
D.lawyer: Knowledge after the theft began, paired with an ordinary gas payment, does not show purposeful aiding of the theft charged.

goldKeys.statement: Accomplice liability requires intent or purpose to promote or facilitate the crime; mere presence, silence, failure to stop, or after-the-fact knowledge is not enough.
goldKeys.trigger: The accused is charged as an accomplice after seeing another person commit the crime.
goldKeys.unlocks: C/D conduct-only traps and A residual

goldKeys.statement: An accomplice is not cleared merely because the principal was not prosecuted or was acquitted.
goldKeys.trigger: Answer points to the principal's prosecution status rather than the accused helper's conduct and mental state.

silverKeys.statement: In accomplice arrays, first separate mental-state answers from conduct-only answers. The conduct may look suspicious, but the accomplice call turns on whether the accused joined the crime on purpose.
silverKeys.trigger: Choices split between intent language and facts about presence, silence, payment, or knowledge.

remediation.title: Accomplice mental-state gate
remediation.signal: Answer says the defendant was present, silent, knew later, or failed to stop the crime.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the answer proves intent to promote the charged offense.
remediation.tinyRule: No intent to promote means no accomplice liability.
remediation.trap: Moral suspicion is not the same as accomplice intent.
